document_title: CBD COP 9 Decision IX/16 C — Ocean Fertilization
notes: CBD COP 9 Decision IX/16 C is the Convention on Biological Diversity's first explicit international policy response to ocean fertilization as a climate-related intervention. It urges Parties and other governments, consistent with the precautionary approach, to ensure that ocean-fertilization activities do not take place until there is an adequate scientific basis for judging the risks and an effective global, transparent and science-based control and regulatory mechanism is in place. The decision allows only small-scale scientific research studies within coastal waters, subject to rigorous prior assessment and only where justified by the need to gather specific scientific data. It also states that such research should not be used for generating or selling carbon offsets or for any other commercial purpose. In the Röschel and Neumann governance review, this decision is part of the direct policy response that complements the London Convention/London Protocol regime. It is a non-binding COP decision: it does not itself issue a project permit, establish a carbon-credit methodology, quantify net CO2 removal, or authorize commercial ocean-fertilization deployment.
source: Convention on Biological Diversity (CBD)
status_note: Adopted by CBD COP 9 in 2008; non-binding international COP decision that remains an important precautionary governance reference for ocean fertilization.

document_title: Resolution LC-LP.1(2008) on the Regulation of Ocean Fertilization
notes: Resolution LC-LP.1(2008) is the first joint London Convention/London Protocol resolution specifically addressing ocean fertilization. The Parties agreed that the scope of the two dumping instruments includes ocean-fertilization activities and concluded that ocean fertilization other than legitimate scientific research should be considered contrary to the aims of the Convention and Protocol and should not currently qualify for an exemption from the definition of dumping. The resolution therefore established a strong precautionary presumption against non-research ocean fertilization while leaving a narrowly framed research pathway to be developed through further assessment rules. Röschel and Neumann identify this resolution as a central component of the direct and explicit international governance of ocean-based negative-emissions technologies. The resolution is policy guidance adopted by Parties rather than a self-executing global project permit. It does not authorize commercial deployment, does not establish removal accounting or carbon-credit issuance, and does not by itself prove the climatic effectiveness or permanence of ocean fertilization.
source: International Maritime Organization (IMO) — London Convention/Protocol
status_note: Adopted jointly by London Convention and London Protocol Parties in 2008; non-binding resolution that remains a core precautionary policy reference for ocean fertilization.

document_title: Resolution LC-LP.2(2010) — Assessment Framework for Scientific Research Involving Ocean Fertilization
notes: Resolution LC-LP.2(2010) adopted the Assessment Framework for Scientific Research Involving Ocean Fertilization. The framework operationalizes the research exception recognized in the 2008 resolution by providing a structured, case-by-case process for deciding whether a proposal qualifies as legitimate scientific research. It requires a scientific rationale, characterization of the proposed activity, environmental assessment, risk management, monitoring, consideration of potential impacts and uncertainties, and follow-up before an activity should proceed. The framework is designed to distinguish genuine scientific research from activities that are effectively commercial or insufficiently justified and to reduce environmental harm while knowledge remains incomplete. Röschel and Neumann highlight this assessment framework as the most developed procedural instrument in the direct governance of ocean-based negative-emissions research. It is an assessment and safeguard framework, not evidence that ocean fertilization is effective at durable net CO2 removal, not a carbon-credit methodology, and not a blanket authorization for field deployment.
source: International Maritime Organization (IMO) — London Convention/Protocol
status_note: Adopted by London Convention/London Protocol Parties in 2010 as the assessment framework for legitimate scientific ocean-fertilization research.

document_title: Report to Congress — Ocean Fertilization: The Potential of Ocean Fertilization for Climate Change Mitigation
notes: NOAA prepared this dedicated Report to Congress on ocean fertilization as a climate-change-mitigation option. The assessment examines deliberate nutrient or iron addition intended to stimulate marine primary production and atmospheric CO2 removal, reviews the evidence for carbon export and air–sea compensation, and considers ecological risks and international governance. NOAA's assessment emphasized that enhanced phytoplankton production had been demonstrated in experiments but that durable deep-ocean transfer and compensating atmospheric CO2 uptake had not been adequately verified, so ocean fertilization was not a mature climate-mitigation technology. The record is included as a direct federal ONCE/mCDR technology-and-governance assessment, not as a deployment authorization, carbon-credit methodology or evidence of successful net removal.
source: U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA)

document_title: Resolution LP.4(8) — Amendment to Regulate Ocean Fertilization and Other Marine Geoengineering
notes: Resolution LP.4(8), adopted in 2013, amends the London Protocol to create a treaty-based control system for marine geoengineering. It adds Article 6bis, establishes a positive-list approach under which marine-geoengineering activities covered by a new annex may not be permitted unless they are listed, and provides an environmental assessment and permitting framework in Annex 5. Ocean fertilization is the first activity listed for regulation, with legitimate scientific research capable of being considered under the assessment framework while other listed activities would require future amendment decisions. The architecture is designed to be expandable to additional marine-geoengineering techniques. Röschel and Neumann treat the amendment as the key prospective international legal structure for governing marine CDR that involves placement of matter in the ocean. The amendment has been adopted but has not entered into force, so its treaty amendments are not yet operative internationally. It does not authorize commercial ocean fertilization, establish carbon-crediting rules, or validate the effectiveness, permanence or net climate benefit of any marine CDR pathway.
source: International Maritime Organization (IMO) — London Protocol
status_note: Adopted in 2013; the marine-geoengineering amendment has not entered into force internationally.

document_title: Marine Microbially Mediated Transformation and Regulation Mechanism of Recalcitrant Dissolved Organic Carbon
notes: This National Key Research and Development Project (2018–2023) is explicitly listed on the Global ONCE website as a Partner's Project. It studies how marine microorganisms transform and regulate recalcitrant dissolved organic carbon (RDOC), with the Microbial Carbon Pump (MCP) as the conceptual framework linking microbial processing to long-term ocean carbon storage. The project connects microbial functional genes, metabolic activity, microbial community succession and dissolved organic matter at molecular and ecosystem scales. It is a concrete funded research project supporting ONCE science rather than a new policy instrument, deployment authorization, MRV standard or carbon-credit methodology.

document_title: Linking Microbial Processes to Costal Deoxygenation AND Carbon Sink Under Global Change

document_title: A Research Strategy for Ocean-based Carbon Dioxide Removal and Sequestration
notes: This National Academies consensus study, publicly released on 8 December 2021, evaluates six broad ocean-based carbon dioxide removal approaches: nutrient fertilization; artificial upwelling and downwelling; seaweed cultivation; marine and coastal ecosystem recovery; ocean alkalinity enhancement; and electrochemical processes. It recommends a USD 125 million cross-cutting research programme over ten years for shared scientific, economic, social, governance and public-engagement questions, while also giving separate pathway-specific research-cost estimates of about USD 290 million for nutrient fertilization, USD 25 million for artificial upwelling/downwelling, USD 130 million for seaweed cultivation, USD 220 million for ecosystem recovery, USD 125–200 million for ocean alkalinity enhancement and USD 350 million for electrochemical processes. These figures are research recommendations rather than a single appropriated federal budget. The report calls for responsible research, permitting and governance work, monitoring and carbon accounting, but it does not authorize deployment, establish carbon credits or conclude that any pathway is ready for climate-scale use. National Academies bibliographic pages commonly list the volume as a 2022 publication, while the formal news release and report highlights are dated December 2021.
source: National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine
status_note: Consensus study publicly released 8 December 2021; National Academies bibliographic metadata also lists the volume as 2022

document_title: CDRmare — Marine Carbon Sinks in Decarbonisation Pathways
notes: CDRmare is a research mission of the German Marine Research Alliance investigating whether and how the ocean can contribute to targeted atmospheric CO2 removal and durable storage. Its initial funding period began in August 2021 with approximately EUR 26 million from Germany's Federal Ministry of Education and Research and involved about 200 researchers across 22 research institutions, authorities and companies. Research covers ocean alkalinity enhancement, vegetated coastal carbon sinks, artificial upwelling, subseabed geological CO2 storage, monitoring and attribution, environmental risks, Earth-system effects, and societal, ethical and legal questions. The mission continues through a later funding phase, but its activities remain research, controlled experimentation and assessment rather than commercial deployment authorization or issuance of carbon credits.

document_title: Global Ocean Negative Carbon Emission (Global ONCE) — UN Ocean Decade Programme
notes: Global Ocean Negative Carbon Emission (Global-ONCE) is an endorsed UN Decade of Ocean Science programme led by Xiamen University, with an official programme period from 1 January 2022 to 31 December 2030. The Ocean Decade description states that the programme will undertake and facilitate the science needed to evaluate and implement eco-technological interventions that could enhance ocean carbon sequestration, including restoration of impacted marine ecosystems, land-sea integrated management, manipulation of upwelling, microbial-driven carbon sequestration, and adjustment of nutrients, dissolved oxygen and pH. Its institutional functions are broader than a single technology project: it is intended to build an international network of field stations and research facilities, co-design interdisciplinary research, develop an evaluation framework for mitigation and adaptation approaches, coordinate capacity building, and improve equitable policy, governance and societal understanding. A 2025 peer-reviewed declaration by early-career ocean professionals describes Global-ONCE as a platform spanning 79 research groups in 33 countries and more than 1,500 participants and calls for stronger basic and applied mCDR research, blue-carbon protection and restoration, international cooperation, monitoring, capacity building and attention to precaution and equity. These descriptions support classification as a research, coordination and evidence-building programme. They do not constitute blanket legal authorization for ocean CDR deployment, do not certify a carbon-credit methodology, and do not establish a quantified programme-wide carbon-removal obligation or guarantee that any intervention will be environmentally acceptable or commercially deployable.
source: UNESCO-IOC Ocean Decade
status_note: Active UN Ocean Decade Programme with an official 1 January 2022–31 December 2030 programme period; it coordinates research, evaluation, capacity building and governance work rather than granting deployment permits or issuing carbon credits.

document_title: Microbes Mediated and Coupled Comprehensive Negative Carbon Emissions in the ocean
notes: This 2022–2025 Special Project of Carbon Neutralization of the National Natural Science Foundation of China, led by Nianzhi Jiao and explicitly listed by Global ONCE as a Partner's Project, uses the marine microbial carbon pump (MCP) as its core theoretical foundation. It studies microbially driven and coupled ocean C, N and S cycles, refractory dissolved organic carbon formation, carbonate and biological pumps, microbial effects on alkalinity and authigenic carbonate formation, and explores microbial-induced carbonate precipitation as a carbon-sequestration technology. The project explicitly aims to propose a verifiable carbon-sink enhancement pathway and scheme for maximizing comprehensive ocean carbon sinks. It is therefore a direct ONCE research-and-engineering programme rather than a general microbial-ecology study.
source: National Natural Science Foundation of China / Global ONCE official Partner's Projects
status_note: NSFC carbon-neutrality special project implemented during 2022–2025; project period has ended.

document_title: Environment Protection (Sea Dumping) Amendment (Using New Technologies to Fight Climate Change) Act 2023 — Marine Geoengineering Research Permitting
notes: Australia's 2023 Sea Dumping amendment became an Act and amended the national sea-dumping framework to enable permits for the placement of wastes or other matter for a marine geoengineering activity for the purpose of scientific research, implementing obligations associated with the 2013 London Protocol marine-geoengineering amendment. For the strict ONCE database, the record is tagged to ocean fertilization because that is the marine-geoengineering activity currently listed under the London Protocol regulatory architecture; the Act is not treated as blanket authorization for OAE, biomass sinking or other emerging mCDR techniques. Its separate provisions concerning export and subseabed storage of captured CO2 are not coded here as marine geological CDR storage because those provisions can also serve conventional point-source CCS and do not by themselves establish a negative-emissions chain. Any research proposal remains subject to permit assessment and environmental safeguards.
source: Parliament of Australia / Australian Government
status_note: Act received Royal Assent in November 2023; project-specific marine-geoengineering research remains subject to the Sea Dumping Act permit and assessment framework.

document_title: NOAA/NOPP Marine Carbon Dioxide Removal Research Partnership — USD 24.3 Million Awards
notes: In September 2023, NOAA's Ocean Acidification Program, acting on behalf of the National Oceanographic Partnership Program, announced USD 24.3 million for 17 marine carbon dioxide removal research projects involving partners from 47 institutions. NOAA reported that USD 14.36 million from the Inflation Reduction Act supported ten projects, while an additional USD 10 million came from NOAA programmes and appropriations together with the Department of Energy, Office of Naval Research, National Science Foundation and ClimateWorks Foundation for seven more projects. The portfolio covers macroalgal cultivation, ocean alkalinity enhancement, enhanced weathering, electrochemical approaches, iron fertilization, field trials, modeling, monitoring, community engagement and ecological-risk research. Its purpose is to reduce uncertainty about efficacy, co-benefits, risks and the science needed for future regulatory frameworks. These are research awards and controlled studies, not a general authorization for commercial mCDR deployment and not a carbon-crediting mechanism. Later Ocean Climate Action Plan progress materials in 2024 highlighted these awards, which can make secondary summaries appear to date the portfolio to 2024; the official NOAA award announcement itself is dated 7 September 2023, so the database year remains 2023 and no duplicate 2024 USD 24 million funding round is created.
source: National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) / National Oceanographic Partnership Program (NOPP)
status_note: USD 24.3 million portfolio announced 7 September 2023; 17 mCDR research projects, with programme activity continuing after award

document_title: NOAA/NOPP Wastewater Alkalinity Enhancement Field Tests — HRSD Virginia Initiative Plant / Elizabeth River
notes: NOAA funded this three-year project to test wastewater alkalinity enhancement at a single Hampton Roads Sanitation District treatment plant in Virginia. The design called for an initial one-week test followed by a four-week test, with controlled alkalinity dosing and monitoring of receiving-water carbon chemistry, oysters, suspended solids, nutrients, metals and other environmental indicators, followed by estuary-ocean modeling. Planetary subsequently reported completion of the two field demonstrations at the Virginia Initiative Plant in Norfolk in 2025. This record represents controlled mCDR research and MRV development; it does not turn conventional wastewater alkalinity dosing into CDR automatically, and it is not a blanket authorization for routine alkalinized discharge.
source: National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) / NOPP / Planetary Technologies / HRSD
status_note: NOAA funded the three-year project across FY2023–2025. Two planned field demonstrations at the HRSD Virginia Initiative Plant were completed by 2025; the project is treated as ended field research, not routine authorized WAE operation.

document_title: SEAO2-CDR — Strategies for the Evaluation and Assessment of Ocean-based Carbon Dioxide Removal
notes: SEAO2-CDR is a Horizon Europe Research and Innovation Action developing evaluation pathways and methodologies for ocean-based carbon dioxide removal. CORDIS records a total cost and EU contribution of EUR 4,443,275, an EC signature date of 17 May 2023, and a project period from 1 June 2023 to 31 May 2027. The project combines technical, economic, legal, political, social and ethical research; develops monitoring, reporting and verification strategies; examines environmental trade-offs and techno-economic viability; and develops governance and business frameworks intended to inform possible future scale-up. It remains a research and method-development programme and has not created binding MRV rules, a carbon-crediting methodology or deployment permits.

document_title: Transforming Climate Action: Addressing the Missing Ocean
notes: Transforming Climate Action: Addressing the Missing Ocean is a major Canada First Research Excellence Fund research initiative led by Dalhousie University with Memorial University of Newfoundland, Université du Québec à Rimouski and Université Laval. The federal CFREF award is CAD 154,414,655, and Dalhousie reported that the grant helps activate a broader research programme approaching CAD 400 million with partner contributions. The initiative focuses on reducing uncertainty in the North Atlantic carbon sink and ocean carbon pump, improving observations and climate prediction, co-designing and evaluating novel ocean-based climate-mitigation approaches, advancing the science and technology of ocean-based carbon dioxide removal, and integrating Indigenous knowledge, justice, equity and community participation into adaptation and governance research. It is a multi-year research and innovation programme, not a deployment permit, carbon-crediting methodology or finding that any specific ocean CDR pathway is ready for commercial scale.

document_title: Ocean Decade Call for Decade Actions No. 10/2025 — Global ONCE and GO-BC Endorsement Window
notes: The Intergovernmental Oceanographic Commission of UNESCO opened Call for Decade Actions No. 10/2025 to invite partners to request Ocean Decade endorsement for programmes, projects and contributions. The call explicitly listed the Global Ocean Negative Carbon Emission programme (Global ONCE) and the Global Ocean Decade Programme for Blue Carbon (GO-BC) among the host programmes to which eligible project proposals could attach, creating a formal international route for new research, observation, capacity-building and solution-oriented actions to enter the Decade network. The window opened in October 2025 and closed in early 2026, so this record captures a completed coordination and endorsement procedure rather than an active funding round. Ocean Decade endorsement is a recognition and alignment mechanism; the call itself did not award research money, approve marine intervention sites, establish legal permission, certify carbon-accounting methods or issue carbon credits. Inclusion of Global ONCE and GO-BC indicates thematic eligibility, not evidence that every submitted or endorsed action removes carbon. Each resulting action requires separate project-level evidence and classification before it can be recorded as research, engineering deployment or a standards-and-market instrument.
source: UNESCO Intergovernmental Oceanographic Commission — United Nations Decade of Ocean Science for Sustainable Development
status_note: Application window closed in early 2026; endorsement decisions and resulting actions require separate project-level records.

document_title: Global ONCE Process-based Certification Mechanism for Ocean Negative Emissions
notes: At COP30 Global ONCE officially presented a proposed process-based certification mechanism for ocean negative emissions. The mechanism responds to the difficulty of directly measuring complex marine carbon-sink outcomes by proposing a whitelist of negative-emission activities and shifting the certification focus toward scientifically verifiable and continuously monitorable carbon-sink enhancement processes. The official account frames it as a pathway toward marine-carbon-sink marketization and global public-good governance. It remains a proposed non-binding mechanism and is not equivalent to an adopted compliance-market methodology or an issued carbon credit.
source: Global ONCE official COP30 outcomes
status_note: Officially proposed by Global ONCE at COP30 in 2025; not yet a binding or universally adopted certification standard.

document_title: Global ONCE Triple REAL Vision
notes: Global ONCE's Triple REAL vision was introduced at the Third UN Ocean Conference in 2025 and presented as the programme's core guiding governance vision at COP30. Global ONCE states that the framework goes beyond conventional MRV by addressing responsibility, sustainability and international acceptability across the full ONCE process. It is a non-binding programme governance framework rather than a treaty or deployment authorization.

document_title: EPA Geoengineering and Marine CDR Regulatory Framework
notes: EPA's current marine geoengineering and marine carbon dioxide removal guidance explains that placing material into ocean waters can trigger federal controls under the Marine Protection, Research, and Sanctuaries Act (MPRSA), while discharges through outfalls or other point sources may instead require Clean Water Act National Pollutant Discharge Elimination System authorization. EPA states that the MPRSA implements U.S. obligations under the London Convention and emphasizes that scientific research involving ocean placement must use a suitable site and robust experimental methods designed to minimize environmental effects. The agency also states that it has serious concerns about proposed marine CDR and solar-radiation-modification activities where environmental performance is unproven, and that no marine geoengineering project has yet met the high threshold necessary to obtain an MPRSA permit. This framework is therefore regulatory and precautionary rather than a blanket authorization for ocean alkalinity enhancement, ocean fertilization, biomass sinking or other interventions. Any individual project remains subject to the applicable statutory pathway, site-specific review, environmental safeguards, public-process requirements and other federal or state approvals. The guidance does not create a carbon-crediting methodology, establish removal factors, certify permanence, or determine whether any specific marine CDR approach is environmentally acceptable.
source: U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA)
status_note: Current EPA regulatory guidance; source page last updated 27 March 2026.

document_title: ISO/DIS 25283-1 — Ships and marine technology — Ocean Negative Carbon Emissions and Carbon Neutrality (ONCE-CN) — Part 1: General guidelines and requirements
notes: ISO/DIS 25283-1 is a draft international standard devoted explicitly to Ocean Negative Carbon Emissions and Carbon Neutrality, making it unusually direct infrastructure for the Global ONCE policy and standards landscape. The draft establishes general guidelines and requirements covering terminology, technical scope, data quality, reporting and assessment for research, development, implementation and evaluation of ocean carbon-sink activities. Its value is not to endorse one intervention, but to create a common vocabulary and minimum information architecture through which different ocean negative-emissions approaches can be described, compared and reported across jurisdictions and organizations. As of 2026 the document remains a Draft International Standard rather than a published ISO standard, so its provisions are still subject to ballot comments and revision. It does not authorize field deployment, establish legally binding environmental thresholds, approve a project, define a complete project-level carbon-credit methodology, or verify that any intervention has achieved durable net removal. Even after publication, conformity with a general standard would not replace technology-specific environmental assessment, monitoring, permitting, life-cycle accounting, additionality, permanence, leakage treatment or social safeguards required by regulators or carbon-crediting programmes.
source: International Organization for Standardization
status_note: Draft International Standard at ISO stage 40.20 in 2026; the DIS ballot was initiated on 6 July 2026 and the text remained under international review.
